content.stem: Radiographic testing forms an image by passing through the part:
options: Penetrating radiation that exposes a film or detector
content.explanation: RT directs X-rays or gamma rays through the part onto a film or digital detector. Differences in how the part absorbs the radiation form an image of the internal structure.
distractors: Sound waves are used in ultrasonic testing, not RT.
A magnetic field is used in magnetic particle testing.
Penetrant is used in PT, not RT.

content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays used in RT are:
content.explanation: Both are high-energy electromagnetic radiation able to ionize atoms. This penetrating, ionizing nature is what lets them image internal structure and also makes them a hazard.
distractors: RT radiation is not sound.
X-rays and gamma rays are far more energetic than visible light.
They are electromagnetic radiation, not magnetic fields.

content.stem: X-rays are produced when:
options: High-speed electrons strike a target in a tube
content.explanation: In an X-ray tube, electrons accelerated from the cathode strike the anode target, producing X-rays. The tube can be switched off, unlike a gamma source.
distractors: Isotope decay produces gamma rays, not tube X-rays.
Sound reflection is unrelated to X-ray production.
Energizing a magnet does not produce X-rays.

content.stem: Gamma rays for RT come from:
options: The decay of a radioactive isotope
content.explanation: Gamma rays are emitted by decaying radioactive isotopes such as iridium-192 or cobalt-60. The source emits continuously and cannot be switched off, only shielded.
distractors: An electrically powered tube produces X-rays, not gamma rays.
A heated filament alone does not produce gamma rays.
Gamma emission is nuclear decay, not a chemical reaction.

content.stem: X-rays and gamma rays differ mainly in their:
content.explanation: Both are electromagnetic radiation of the same fundamental nature; they differ in origin (tube versus isotope) and typically in energy range.
distractors: Both travel at the speed of light in vacuum.
Neither is sound; both are electromagnetic radiation.
Neither is defined by a visible color.

content.stem: The radiographic image forms because different parts of the object:
options: Reflect the radiation back to the source
content.explanation: Thicker or denser regions absorb more radiation and pass less to the film; thinner or less dense regions pass more. These differences create the image.
distractors: The image comes from differential absorption, not reflection back to the source.
Vibration is the basis of ultrasonic testing, not radiographic imaging.
Magnetization is unrelated to the radiographic image.

content.stem: On a processed film radiograph, an area that received more radiation appears:
content.explanation: More radiation reaching the film produces more development and a darker area. Less radiation gives a lighter area.
distractors: More radiation gives a darker, not lighter, area.
More radiation does change the film density.
Film density is shades of gray, not color.

content.stem: A gas pore or void in steel typically shows on the radiograph as a:
options: Darker spot than the surrounding metal
Lighter spot than the surrounding metal
content.explanation: A void is less material in the beam path, so more radiation passes through and the area is darker than the surrounding solid metal.
distractors: Less material passes more radiation, giving a darker, not lighter, spot.
Radiographs are grayscale, not colored.
A void changes the local absorption and does show.

content.stem: A dense tungsten inclusion in an aluminum or steel weld typically shows as a:
options: Lighter area than the surrounding metal
Darker area than the surrounding metal
content.explanation: A denser inclusion absorbs more radiation than the surrounding metal, so less reaches the film and the area is lighter.
distractors: A denser inclusion passes less radiation, giving a lighter, not darker, area.
Radiographs are grayscale, not colored.
A density difference does produce an indication.

content.stem: Higher-energy radiation (higher kV or a higher-energy isotope) is generally:
content.explanation: Higher photon energy penetrates thicker or denser material. Lower energy penetrates less but can give higher contrast on thinner sections.
distractors: Higher energy penetrates more, not less.
All such radiation travels at the speed of light; energy does not change its speed.
Radiation used in RT is not audible.

content.stem: For electromagnetic radiation, higher energy corresponds to:
content.explanation: Higher-energy photons have shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies. Shorter wavelength radiation tends to be more penetrating.
distractors: Higher energy means shorter, not longer, wavelength.
Electromagnetic radiation does have a wavelength.
Higher energy means higher, not lower, frequency.

content.stem: Common industrial gamma-ray sources include:
content.explanation: Iridium-192, cobalt-60, and selenium-75 are common sealed gamma sources, each suited to a range of material thicknesses. Lead and tungsten are shielding or target materials, not sources.
distractors: Aluminum and copper are structural metals, not gamma sources.
Hydrogen and helium are not industrial gamma sources.
Lead and tungsten are used for shielding and targets, not as gamma sources.

content.stem: The half-life of a radioactive source is the time for its:
options: Activity to decrease to half its value
content.explanation: Activity falls by half each half-life, so output decreases over time and exposures must be lengthened as the source ages.
distractors: Half-life concerns decreasing activity, not doubling energy.
The source mass does not vanish at the half-life.
Half-life is about activity, not color.

content.stem: Iridium-192 has a half-life of roughly:
content.explanation: Iridium-192's half-life is about 74 days, so its activity drops noticeably over weeks and exposure times must be recalculated as it decays. Confirm exact values against source data.
distractors: Iridium-192 does not decay in minutes.
Its half-life is far less than 100 years.
Its half-life is far longer than an hour.

content.stem: Cobalt-60, used for thick steel, has a half-life of roughly:
content.explanation: Cobalt-60's half-life is about 5.3 years and its high energy suits thick sections. Confirm exact values against the source data.
distractors: Cobalt-60's half-life is years, not days.
Its half-life is years, not minutes.
Its half-life is about 5.3 years, not centuries.

content.stem: Source activity is measured in:
content.explanation: Activity, the rate of decay, is expressed in becquerels (SI) or curies. One curie equals 3.7 times ten to the tenth becquerels.
distractors: Volts and amperes are electrical units, used for X-ray tubes, not activity.
Meters and feet are distances, not activity.
Degrees measure angle or temperature, not activity.

content.stem: A higher-energy source such as cobalt-60 is chosen for:
content.explanation: High-energy cobalt-60 penetrates thick steel. Lower-energy sources like selenium-75 or iridium-192 suit thinner sections with better contrast.
distractors: Thin sections are better served by lower-energy sources for contrast.
RT is used on metals and other materials, not nonmetals only.
A high-energy source increases, not reduces, penetration.

content.stem: Selenium-75 is generally selected for:
options: Thinner steel sections needing good detail
content.explanation: Selenium-75's lower energy gives good contrast and detail on thinner steel, where cobalt-60 would be too penetrating. Confirm thickness ranges against the procedure.
distractors: Very thick castings favor higher-energy sources.
Selenium-75 does not remove the need for shielding.
Selenium-75 is an ionizing radiation source.

content.stem: Radiation used in RT travels:
options: In straight lines from the source
Randomly in all directions equally after the part
content.explanation: Radiation travels in straight lines from the source, which is why geometry (source size and distances) controls image sharpness and magnification.
distractors: The primary beam travels in straight lines, not curves.
It penetrates the volume, not just the surface.
The primary beam is directional; scatter is a separate, unwanted effect.

content.stem: Unlike surface methods, RT can reveal:
content.explanation: RT is a volumetric method that images internal features such as porosity, inclusions, and lack of fusion, as well as some surface conditions.
distractors: RT is not limited to surface cracks.
RT works on nonmagnetic materials too.
RT images density differences, not color.

content.stem: A traditional advantage of film radiography is that it provides:
options: A permanent record image of the inspection
content.explanation: A processed radiograph is a retainable image record of the part at the time of inspection. Digital RT also stores retrievable image records.
distractors: RT does not produce sound.
RT does not give a magnetic reading.
A penetrant trace belongs to PT.

content.stem: Radiation passing through material is reduced by:
content.explanation: The beam is attenuated as photons are absorbed and scattered. Thicker, denser material attenuates more, which forms the image and also requires more exposure.
distractors: Magnetization does not attenuate the radiation beam.
Evaporation is unrelated to beam attenuation.
Sound refraction is an ultrasonic effect, not RT attenuation.

content.stem: Scattered radiation reaching the film tends to:
options: Degrade image quality by adding unwanted exposure
content.explanation: Scatter adds nondirectional exposure that lowers contrast and clarity, so it is controlled with lead screens, collimation, masking, and backscatter protection.
distractors: Scatter blurs rather than sharpens the image.
Scatter reduces, not adds, useful contrast.
Scatter does affect image quality and is controlled.

content.stem: Before processing, the exposed film holds a:
options: Latent image that processing makes visible
content.explanation: Exposure creates an invisible latent image in the emulsion; development converts it into a visible density pattern.
distractors: The image is latent (invisible) until processed.
The film holds a latent photochemical image, not a magnetic one.
Film does not record sound.

content.stem: RT most readily detects a discontinuity that produces a:
options: Detectable change in absorption along the beam direction
content.explanation: A flaw that changes the amount of material (and thus absorption) along the beam shows as a density change. Flaws with little thickness change in the beam direction can be hard to detect.
distractors: RT responds to absorption changes, not surface color.
Magnetic leakage is the basis of MT, not RT.
Sound echoes are the basis of UT, not RT.

content.stem: A tight crack is most likely to be detected by RT when it is:
options: Aligned roughly parallel to the radiation beam
content.explanation: A crack aligned with the beam presents a measurable gap along the beam path and shows as a line. A crack across the beam may change absorption too little to detect.
distractors: A crack across the beam may not change absorption enough to show.
A crack is a gap, not the same metal; that is why it shows.
Position relative to the beam, not below the film, governs detectability.

content.stem: On an X-ray tube, the kilovoltage (kV) mainly controls the radiation's:
content.explanation: kV sets the energy (penetrating power) of the X-rays. The tube current (mA) and time set the quantity of radiation.
distractors: Quantity is set mainly by mA and time, not kV.
kV does not set a color.
kV does not produce sound.

content.stem: On an X-ray tube, the milliamperage (mA) mainly controls the radiation's:
content.explanation: mA sets how much radiation is produced per unit time; kV sets the energy. Together with time they determine the exposure.
distractors: Penetrating energy is set by kV, not mA.
Wavelength relates to energy (kV), not mA.
Direction is set by the tube and collimator, not mA.

content.stem: Unlike an X-ray tube, a gamma source:
options: Cannot be switched off and must be shielded
content.explanation: A gamma isotope emits continuously and is controlled only by shielding and distance, never an off switch, which shapes how it is stored and handled.
distractors: A gamma source cannot be turned off electrically.
It emits continuously, not only when powered.
A gamma source is a significant radiation hazard.

content.stem: As a gamma source ages over months, its output:
options: Decreases, so exposure times must increase
content.explanation: Because activity halves each half-life, output falls and exposures are lengthened over time, using the current source activity.
distractors: Output decreases, not increases, with age.
Output changes with decay; it is not constant.
The source remains ionizing as it decays.

content.stem: In radiography, beam quality refers to penetrating energy and beam quantity refers to:
content.explanation: Quality is the energy (penetration); quantity is how much radiation is delivered. Both are set to give a proper exposure.
distractors: Penetrating energy is beam quality, not quantity.
Wavelength relates to energy (quality), not quantity.
Focal-spot size affects sharpness, not the quantity of radiation.

content.stem: Ionizing radiation is hazardous because it can:
content.explanation: Ionizing radiation can damage cells and tissue, which is why exposure is minimized and strictly controlled. This hazard drives all RT safety practice.
distractors: The hazard is biological damage, not harmless warming.
Radiation does not magnetize blood.
Radiation is not heard as sound.

content.stem: Image quality in radiography is verified using a device called a:
content.explanation: An image quality indicator (IQI, or penetrameter) demonstrates the radiographic sensitivity achieved. Other devices serve measurement, safety, or beam-shaping roles.
distractors: A densitometer measures film density; it is not the image quality indicator placed in the beam.
A survey meter measures radiation levels, not image quality.
A collimator shapes the beam; it does not indicate image quality.

content.stem: Film density in radiography refers to:
options: The degree of darkening of the processed film
content.explanation: Radiographic density is the degree of film blackening, measured with a densitometer. Acceptable density ranges are set by the code or procedure.
distractors: Density here is film darkening, not the part's mass.
It is not the hardness of the material.
It is film darkening, not source activity.

content.stem: Radiographic contrast is the:
options: Difference in density between two areas of the image
content.explanation: Contrast is the density difference that makes features visible. It comes from subject contrast (material and energy) and film contrast (film and processing).
distractors: Overall darkness is density, not contrast.
Film speed is a separate property from contrast.
Half-life is a source property, not image contrast.

content.stem: Using higher kV (higher energy) generally produces:
options: Lower subject contrast but more penetration
content.explanation: Higher energy penetrates more but flattens the density differences, lowering subject contrast. Lower energy raises contrast but penetrates less.
distractors: Higher kV lowers contrast and increases penetration, not the reverse.
kV does change the contrast.
Higher kV does not make audible output.

content.stem: Besides film, modern RT can record the image using:
content.explanation: Computed radiography (imaging plates) and digital radiography (direct detectors) capture the image electronically, offering quick viewing and digital storage.
distractors: RT does not record sound on magnetic tape.
Penetrant film is not an RT image medium.
A pie gauge is a magnetic particle field indicator, not an RT detector.

content.stem: A smaller radiation source or focal spot generally gives:
content.explanation: A smaller source acts more like a point, reducing geometric unsharpness and giving sharper images. A large source increases blur.
distractors: A smaller source reduces, not increases, blur.
Images are visual, not loud.
RT does not produce magnetic indications.

content.stem: Interpreting and evaluating radiographs against acceptance criteria is generally the job of a:
content.explanation: A Level I makes the exposure, processes, and records under direction. Interpreting and accepting or rejecting against the code is a Level II or higher responsibility.
distractors: Evaluation to criteria is above the Level I scope.
The film supplier provides materials, not evaluations.
Evaluation is a qualified-personnel task, not a janitorial one.

content.stem: Which statement about RT fundamentals is correct?
options: Penetrating radiation forms an image from absorption differences, and it is an ionizing hazard
RT uses sound to image the surface
RT works only on magnetic parts
content.explanation: RT uses ionizing X-rays or gamma rays that are absorbed differently by the part to form a volumetric image, and the radiation is a hazard that must be controlled.
distractors: RT uses penetrating radiation, not sound, and images the volume.
RT is not limited to magnetic parts.
Ionizing radiation is a real health hazard.

content.stem: The two principal electrodes of an X-ray tube are the:
content.explanation: Electrons leave the heated cathode filament and strike the anode target, producing X-rays. The pigtail and projector belong to gamma equipment.
distractors: The source pellet and pigtail belong to a gamma source assembly, not an X-ray tube.
A collimator and filter shape and condition the beam; they are not the tube electrodes.
Cassette and screen hold and intensify the film; they are not tube electrodes.

content.stem: In an X-ray tube, the cathode:
options: Supplies the electrons by heating a filament
content.explanation: The heated cathode filament emits electrons that are accelerated to the target. X-rays are produced at the anode target.
distractors: X-rays are produced at the anode target, not the cathode.
Beam shaping is done by the collimator, not the cathode.
The cathode does not hold film.

content.stem: X-rays are produced at the X-ray tube's:
content.explanation: Electrons striking the high-atomic-number target (often tungsten) produce X-rays. Most of the energy becomes heat, so cooling is needed.
distractors: The cathode emits electrons; X-rays form at the target.
Cooling fins remove heat; they do not produce X-rays.
The power cord supplies energy; it does not produce X-rays.

content.stem: The focal spot of an X-ray tube is the:
options: Area of the target where X-rays originate
content.explanation: The focal spot is where the beam effectively originates. A smaller focal spot reduces geometric unsharpness and gives sharper images.
distractors: The film center is not the focal spot.
The collimator opening shapes the beam; it is not the focal spot.
The guide tube tip is gamma equipment, not the X-ray focal spot.

content.stem: A smaller focal spot generally produces:
options: Sharper images with less geometric unsharpness
content.explanation: A small focal spot behaves more like a point source, reducing penumbra and sharpening detail. It does not by itself change kV.
distractors: A smaller focal spot reduces, not increases, blur.
Focal spot size is separate from the amount of scatter generated.
Focal spot size does not set the kV.

content.stem: X-ray tube targets are commonly made of a high-atomic-number metal such as:
content.explanation: Tungsten is common because its high atomic number and high melting point suit efficient X-ray production and heat tolerance.
distractors: Aluminum is low atomic number and a poor target choice.
Plastic cannot serve as an X-ray target.
Magnesium is low atomic number and unsuitable as a target.

content.stem: An industrial gamma source is a:
options: Sealed capsule of radioactive material on a drive cable (pigtail)
content.explanation: The sealed source sits in a capsule attached to a drive cable (pigtail) and is moved out of its shield for exposure. It is never open or loose.
distractors: A heated filament is part of an X-ray tube, not a gamma source.
Gamma sources are sealed, never an open liquid.
Gamma sources are sealed capsules, not loose powder.

content.stem: The shielded container that stores a gamma source and lets it be cranked out is the:
content.explanation: The exposure device shields the source in storage and, with a drive cable, moves it through a guide tube to the exposure position.
distractors: A densitometer measures film density, not a source container.
A cassette holds film, not the gamma source.
A step wedge is a density reference, not a source container.

content.stem: The shielding inside a gamma exposure device is usually made of:
content.explanation: Dense, high-atomic-number depleted uranium or tungsten provides compact shielding for the source in storage and transport.
distractors: Plastic foam provides negligible gamma shielding.
Aluminum foil is far too thin and light to shield gamma rays.
Cardboard provides no meaningful gamma shielding.

content.stem: A drive cable and crank assembly are used to:
options: Move the source out remotely so the operator stays at a distance
content.explanation: Remote crank-out lets the operator expose the source from a safe distance through the drive cable and guide tube, reducing dose.
distractors: Gamma sources are not heated to operate.
Beam collimation is the collimator's job, not the drive cable's.
Tube cooling applies to X-ray units, not gamma crank-out.

content.stem: The guide tube on a gamma exposure device:
options: Directs the source to the exposure position
Stores the source when not in use
content.explanation: The guide tube routes the source from the device to the collimator or exposure head at the part, keeping the path controlled.
distractors: Radiation is measured by a survey meter, not the guide tube.
Source storage is the shielded device body's role, not the guide tube's.
Focal spot is an X-ray tube property, not set by a guide tube.

content.stem: A collimator on the source is used to:
options: Restrict the beam to the area of interest, reducing scatter and dose
content.explanation: Collimating confines the beam to the needed area, improving image quality by cutting scatter and reducing radiation in surrounding areas.
distractors: A collimator reduces, not increases, scatter.
Focal-spot size is a tube property, not set by the collimator.
A collimator does not magnetize the part.

content.stem: Iridium-192 is widely used because its energy suits:
options: A moderate range of steel thicknesses
content.explanation: Iridium-192's energy range handles a broad span of moderate steel thicknesses, making it a versatile field source. Confirm thickness limits against the procedure.
distractors: Iridium-192 is not limited to paper-thin sections.
Very thick sections often need higher-energy cobalt-60.
RT covers metals broadly, not nonmetals exclusively.

content.stem: Cobalt-60 emits relatively high-energy gamma rays near:
content.explanation: Cobalt-60's two gamma energies near 1.17 and 1.33 MeV penetrate thick steel. Confirm values against source data.
distractors: Cobalt-60's energies are far above 1 keV.
10 eV is far too low for cobalt-60 gamma rays.
A gamma source emits energetic photons, not zero energy.

content.stem: A radiation survey meter is essential equipment used to:
options: Measure radiation levels and confirm the source is shielded
content.explanation: A calibrated survey meter verifies radiation levels, confirms the source has returned to its shielded position, and helps define safe boundaries.
distractors: Sources are not charged; their activity comes from decay.
kV is set on the X-ray control, not by a survey meter.
The IQI is placed in the beam; the survey meter does not hold it.

content.stem: After each gamma exposure, the operator must:
options: Survey to confirm the source returned to its shielded position
Open the device immediately by hand
content.explanation: A survey after every exposure confirms the source is fully shielded before anyone approaches. Never assume the source returned without confirming.
distractors: The source position is confirmed by survey, never assumed.
Opening the device by hand near an unshielded source is dangerous.
The post-exposure survey is mandatory, not skipped.

content.stem: Portable X-ray units are used because they:
options: Can be taken to the part in the field or shop
content.explanation: Portable units bring the X-ray source to the work. They still require power and emit radiation that must be controlled.
distractors: Portable units are designed to be moved, not fixed.
X-ray units require electrical power.
X-ray units emit ionizing radiation when energized.

content.stem: A panoramic exposure places the source so the beam radiates:
options: Outward in all directions, exposing a full circumference at once
In a single narrow line only
content.explanation: A panoramic setup centers the source in a cylinder (such as a pipe) to expose the whole circumference in one shot, improving efficiency.
distractors: A directional or single-wall shot covers a limited area, unlike panoramic.
The beam radiates outward to the part, not back to the source.
Panoramic exposure radiates in all directions, not only downward.

content.stem: X-ray tubes require cooling because:
options: Most of the electron energy becomes heat at the target
content.explanation: Only a small fraction of the electron energy becomes X-rays; the rest is heat, so duty cycles and cooling protect the tube.
distractors: Film is not what overheats the tube.
The collimator is not the source of the heat that requires cooling.
Cooling addresses heat, not freezing of the cathode.

content.stem: Before use, gamma exposure equipment should be:
options: Inspected for cable, connector, and lock condition
content.explanation: Worn drive cables, bad connectors, or a faulty source lock can cause a stuck or exposed source, so equipment is inspected and maintained before use.
distractors: Faulty equipment can cause a source accident.
Safety is verified, not assumed.
Field disassembly of the source device is not a routine practice.

content.stem: The lock on a gamma exposure device exists to:
options: Secure the source in the shielded position against unauthorized or accidental movement
content.explanation: Locking the source in its shield prevents accidental or unauthorized exposure and is part of source security.
distractors: The lock secures the source; it does not increase output.
Dose rate is measured by a survey meter, not the lock.
Beam shaping is the collimator's role, not the lock's.

content.stem: Selenium-75 emits lower-energy gamma rays than iridium-192, which makes it suited to:
content.explanation: Selenium-75's lower energy improves contrast and detail on thinner steel, where it outperforms iridium-192. Confirm ranges against the procedure.
distractors: The thickest sections favor higher-energy sources.
Selenium-75 still requires shielding.
Selenium-75 is an ionizing source.

content.stem: When not in use, gamma sources are kept in:
content.explanation: Sources are stored shielded and secured against theft or loss, with access controlled and inventory maintained.
distractors: An open shelf provides no shielding or security.
A film cassette holds film, not a gamma source.
A darkroom sink is for processing, not source storage.

content.stem: A very small focal spot improves sharpness but can limit:
options: The tube output (heat loading), affecting exposure time
content.explanation: Concentrating electrons on a tiny spot raises heat there, limiting the current and lengthening exposures, a trade-off against sharpness.
distractors: Focal spot size does not set the film size.
The safelight is unrelated to focal spot size.
IQI material is not affected by focal spot size.

content.stem: On an X-ray control panel, the operator sets the:
content.explanation: The operator selects kV (energy), mA (intensity), and time on the control to give the required exposure. Half-life and isotope energy apply to gamma sources, not an X-ray panel.
distractors: Half-life is a property of gamma isotopes, not an X-ray panel setting.
Film grain is a film property, not a panel setting.
Isotope energy applies to gamma sources, not an X-ray tube panel.

content.stem: A metal filter placed at the X-ray tube port is sometimes used to:
options: Absorb low-energy radiation and harden the beam
content.explanation: Filtration removes softer (low-energy) photons, hardening the beam and reducing some scatter, which can improve image quality on certain work.
distractors: A filter reduces scatter rather than adding it.
A filter does not cool the cathode.
A filter conditions the beam energy; it does not magnify the image.

content.stem: A source changer is used to:
options: Safely transfer a source between devices behind shielding
content.explanation: Source changers allow shielded transfer and replacement of sources, performed by qualified personnel following strict procedures.
distractors: A source changer is unrelated to film development.
kV is an X-ray setting, not a source-changer function.
Film marking is a separate identification step.

content.stem: A gamma source on its pigtail must:
options: Never be handled directly by hand
Be picked up quickly by hand
content.explanation: Direct contact with an unshielded source can cause severe, rapid radiation injury, so sources are handled only remotely with proper tools and shielding.
distractors: Handling a source by hand, even quickly, can cause severe injury.
Carrying a source in a pocket would deliver a dangerous dose.
A source is never wiped or touched by hand.

content.stem: Some X-ray tubes require warm-up (seasoning) to:
options: Condition the tube and prevent damage at high kV
content.explanation: Gradual warm-up conditions the tube and reduces the risk of arcing or damage when stepping up to high kV after idle periods.
distractors: Warm-up conditions the tube; it does not sharpen the focal spot.
X-ray tubes have no isotope to charge.
Warm-up is a tube procedure; it does not change film speed.

content.stem: A directional exposure device emits the beam:
options: In a specific direction toward the area of interest
content.explanation: A directional setup aims the beam at a chosen area, unlike a panoramic shot that radiates all around. Both deliver ionizing radiation, not light or sound.
distractors: Radiating in all directions describes a panoramic, not directional, exposure.
The beam is ionizing radiation, not visible light.
The beam is radiation, not sound.

content.stem: A worn or kinked drive cable is dangerous because it can:
options: Cause the source to stick out of its shield
content.explanation: A damaged cable can fail to retract the source, leaving it exposed, which is a serious radiation emergency, so cables are inspected and maintained.
distractors: A worn cable is a safety hazard, not an image-quality benefit.
Cable condition does not set kV.
Cable condition is unrelated to processing speed.

content.stem: Selecting the radiation source or kV is based mainly on the:
options: Material and thickness to be penetrated
The length of the drive cable
content.explanation: Penetration must match the material and thickness, so energy (kV or isotope choice) is selected accordingly, within the procedure.
distractors: Film size is chosen for coverage, not the basis for energy selection.
Ambient light does not drive source or kV selection.
Drive-cable length is an equipment detail, not the basis for energy selection.

content.stem: With sources and equipment, the Level I technician is generally expected to:
options: Operate and inspect equipment and follow procedures under direction
content.explanation: A Level I operates and checks the equipment and follows procedures under direction; design, licensing, and limit-setting are higher-level or regulatory functions.
distractors: Designing exposure devices is not a Level I function.
Licensing approval is a regulatory and management function.
Dose limits are set by regulators, not the Level I.

content.stem: Which statement about RT sources and equipment is correct?
options: X-ray tubes produce radiation electrically and switch off; gamma devices use a sealed source that is only shielded
Gamma sources can be switched off electrically
X-ray tubes use a radioactive pellet
content.explanation: X-ray tubes make radiation when powered and stop when off; gamma exposure devices shield a continuously emitting sealed source and move it out remotely for exposure.
distractors: Gamma sources cannot be switched off; they are only shielded.
X-ray tubes produce radiation electrically, not from a radioactive pellet.
Both X-ray and gamma equipment emit a radiation hazard.

content.stem: Radiographic film consists of an emulsion of light-sensitive material coated on a:
options: Transparent base, usually on both sides
content.explanation: The emulsion (silver halide in gelatin) is coated on a clear base, typically both sides, to capture the image. The base is film, not lead or developer.
distractors: Lead is used for screens, not the film base.
Developer is a processing chemical, not the film base.
A fluorescent screen is a separate item, not the film base.

content.stem: The light- and radiation-sensitive compound in film emulsion is a:
content.explanation: Silver halide crystals form the latent image when exposed; development converts exposed crystals to metallic silver.
distractors: Lead oxide is not the imaging compound in film emulsion.
Copper sulfate is not the film's sensitive compound.
Carbon powder is not the imaging compound.

content.stem: Compared with slow, fine-grain film, fast film generally has:
options: Larger grain, shorter exposure, and less definition
content.explanation: Faster film uses larger grains, needing less exposure but giving coarser detail. Fine-grain film gives finer detail and contrast but needs longer exposure.
distractors: Finer grain and more definition describe slow, not fast, film.
Film speed strongly affects exposure time.
Fast film gives lower, not higher, resolution.

content.stem: Fine-grain (slow) film is chosen when the job needs:
options: High detail and contrast, accepting longer exposure
content.explanation: Fine-grain film resolves small features with good contrast at the cost of exposure time, used where image quality is critical.
distractors: The shortest exposure favors faster, coarser film.
Fine-grain film gives more, not less, detail.
Film is chosen to produce an image, not none.

content.stem: Lead intensifying screens placed against the film:
options: Intensify the image and absorb scatter, improving quality
content.explanation: Under radiation, lead screens emit electrons that add to the film exposure (intensifying) and absorb scattered radiation, improving image quality, when in tight contact.
distractors: Lead screens condition the beam reaching the film; they do not block all radiation.
Screens do not cool the cassette.
Screens work with the cassette; they do not replace it.

content.stem: Lead screens must be in close, uniform contact with the film because poor contact causes:
content.explanation: Gaps between screen and film blur the image. Cassettes (sometimes vacuum types) maintain tight contact for sharp results.
distractors: Poor contact blurs rather than sharpens.
Contact does not change development speed.
Screen contact does not change the source energy.

content.stem: Fluorescent screens differ from lead screens in that they:
options: Emit light to expose the film, giving speed but less definition
Emit no light and add detail
content.explanation: Fluorescent screens glow under radiation to expose film quickly, but their light spread lowers definition, so they are used where speed outweighs fine detail.
distractors: Fluorescent screens emit light and reduce definition, not add detail.
Screens do not harden the beam; filtration does.
Screens are not operator shielding.

content.stem: A film cassette or holder is used to:
options: Hold the film and screens in light-tight, close contact
content.explanation: The cassette keeps film and screens together, flat, and shielded from light until processing. It does not measure radiation or operate the source.
distractors: Radiation is measured by a survey meter, not the cassette.
kV is set on the control panel, not the cassette.
The source is moved by the exposure device, not the cassette.

content.stem: Film is loaded and unloaded:
options: In a darkroom under appropriate safelight
content.explanation: Film is light-sensitive, so it is handled in a darkroom with a safelight that does not fog it. White light or sunlight would ruin it.
distractors: Bright white light fogs the film.
Sunlight fogs the film.
Handling film under the beam would expose and ruin it.

content.stem: Film should be handled by its edges to avoid:
content.explanation: Pressure, bending, fingerprints, and static can leave artifacts that mimic or hide indications, so film is handled carefully by the edges.
distractors: Careless handling adds artifacts; it does not improve contrast.
Rough handling harms, not improves, sharpness.
Film handling has nothing to do with charging an isotope.

content.stem: Pulling film quickly from its packaging in a dry room can cause:
options: Static discharge marks on the film
content.explanation: Static from rapid handling, especially in low humidity, can expose the emulsion in branch-like marks, so film is handled gently.
distractors: Static marks are artifacts, not a contrast improvement.
Static does not speed development.
Film handling does not change the beam.

content.stem: Computed radiography (CR) captures the image on a:
content.explanation: CR uses an imaging plate that stores the latent image, then is scanned by a laser to read it out and erased for reuse.
distractors: CR uses an imaging plate, not pre-developed film.
A lead screen alone does not capture the CR image.
A survey meter measures radiation, not the image.

content.stem: Digital radiography (DR) uses a:
options: Direct flat-panel detector that produces a digital image
content.explanation: DR flat-panel detectors convert radiation directly to a digital image viewable almost immediately, without film processing.
distractors: DR avoids wet film processing.
Penetrant is a PT material, not a DR detector.
A particle bath is an MT material, not a DR detector.

content.stem: An advantage of digital RT over film is:
options: Quick image viewing and digital storage
content.explanation: Digital systems display images quickly and store them electronically. They still use ionizing radiation and require full safety controls.
distractors: Digital RT still uses ionizing radiation.
Radiation safety still fully applies to digital RT.
Digital RT still requires a detector to form the image.

content.stem: A CR imaging plate, after being read, is:
content.explanation: After laser readout, the plate is erased with bright light and reused many times, unlike single-use film.
distractors: Imaging plates are reused, not discarded each time.
Plates are not processed in fixer like film.
Plates are erased and reused, not melted.

content.stem: Film latitude refers to the range of thicknesses or exposures that produce:
options: Acceptable density on a single radiograph
content.explanation: Wide-latitude film records a broader range of thickness in one exposure; high-contrast film has narrower latitude but greater sensitivity to small changes.
distractors: Latitude is a range, not one fixed density.
Latitude still produces an image within the range.
Latitude concerns density range, not grain size.

content.stem: Unexposed film should be stored:
options: Cool and dry, away from radiation and chemicals, within shelf life
content.explanation: Heat, humidity, stray radiation, chemical fumes, and age all fog or degrade film, so it is stored properly and used within its shelf life.
distractors: Storing film near a source fogs it.
Heat and humidity degrade film.
Sunlight exposes and ruins film.

content.stem: The thickness of lead screens is selected mainly for the:
options: The film size in the cassette
content.explanation: Screen thickness is matched to the radiation energy so it intensifies and filters scatter effectively without over-absorbing the useful beam.
distractors: Film size does not set the screen thickness.
Exposure time does not set the screen thickness.
Source-to-film distance is a geometry factor, not the basis for screen thickness.

content.stem: Most industrial film is coated with emulsion on both sides to:
options: Increase speed and density for a given exposure
content.explanation: Two emulsion layers capture more of the radiation, increasing speed and density compared with a single-sided coating.
distractors: Double coating increases, not reduces, sensitivity.
Film must remain translucent for viewing, not opaque.
The base remains; emulsion is coated on it.

content.stem: Unwanted overall darkening (fog) on film can come from:
options: Heat, age, stray radiation, or light leaks
content.explanation: Fog reduces contrast and can mask indications; its sources include heat, outdated film, stray radiation, chemical contamination, and light leaks.
distractors: Correct exposure forms the image, not fog.
Proper storage prevents, rather than causes, fog.
A clean darkroom helps prevent fog.

content.stem: A vacuum cassette is used to:
options: Ensure tight film-to-screen contact for sharpness
content.explanation: Drawing a vacuum presses film and screens into uniform contact, reducing blur from gaps, useful on larger or curved work.
distractors: A vacuum cassette reduces blur; it does not add scatter.
A cassette does not collimate the beam.
It does not power the tube.

content.stem: Film and digital systems are grouped into classes mainly by their:
options: Image quality characteristics such as grain and contrast
content.explanation: System classes describe image quality (for example grain, contrast, and signal-to-noise), so a procedure can specify a class adequate for the work.
distractors: Cassette dimensions do not define a film system class.
Exposure time is a technique choice, not a system-class basis.
Source-to-film distance is geometry, not a film-class basis.

content.stem: In a typical lead-screen setup, screens are placed:
options: In front of and behind the film
content.explanation: Front and back lead screens sandwich the film, intensifying the image and absorbing scatter from both sides.
distractors: Screens are in the cassette at exposure, not stored only in the darkroom.
Screens are not placed inside the tube.
Screens are not placed around the survey meter.

content.stem: Screens and cassettes should be kept clean because dirt or scratches can:
options: Appear as artifacts on every radiograph taken with them
content.explanation: A scratch or speck on a screen prints onto each radiograph, so screens are inspected and kept clean to avoid recurring false indications.
distractors: Dirt creates artifacts, not better contrast.
Cleanliness does not change development speed.
Screen condition does not change source energy.

content.stem: In digital RT, image quality is partly described by:
content.explanation: Digital image quality depends on signal-to-noise and resolution. Grain, developer, and fixer are film-processing concepts, not digital ones.
distractors: Grain size is a film concept, not digital.
Developer temperature is a film-processing parameter.
Fixer strength is a film-processing parameter.

content.stem: Very fast film is not always used because it:
options: Sacrifices image detail and may miss small flaws
content.explanation: Speed trades away definition, so critical work uses finer-grain, slower film to resolve small discontinuities despite longer exposures.
distractors: Fast film does form an image, just with less detail.
Fast film still requires exposure.
Fast film gives less, not the best, detail.

content.stem: Each radiograph must carry identification so it can be:
options: Traced to the part, location, and date
content.explanation: Permanent identification (often lead letters imaged on the film) ties the radiograph to the specific part, weld location, and date for traceability.
distractors: Radiographs are records, not items for public sale.
Identified radiographs are records, not scrap.
Anonymous film cannot be traced and is not acceptable.

content.stem: A key difference between CR and DR is that CR uses a separate plate that is:
options: Scanned after exposure, while DR reads out directly
content.explanation: CR exposes a plate then scans it in a reader; DR detectors digitize directly at exposure. CR plates are reusable.
distractors: CR plates are reusable, not single-use.
Imaging plates are phosphor-based, not penetrant.
The plate is not powered by the source.

content.stem: With film and image media, the Level I technician:
options: Handles, loads, and processes media and records results under direction
content.explanation: A Level I handles and processes the media and records results; criteria, procedures, and system qualification are higher-level functions.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Writing procedures is above the Level I.
System certification is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: Which statement about RT image media is correct?
options: Film records a latent image developed later; lead screens intensify and reduce scatter; digital media store images electronically
Faster film always gives the best detail
content.explanation: Film captures a latent image processed later, lead screens improve quality, and digital systems (CR and DR) capture and store images electronically while still using radiation.
distractors: Faster film gives less detail, not the best.
Lead screens improve the image; they do not develop the film.
Digital RT still uses ionizing radiation.

content.stem: The main exposure factors in radiography are radiation energy, intensity, time, and:
content.explanation: Energy (kV or isotope), intensity (mA or activity), time, and distance together set the exposure and the resulting density.
distractors: Film size affects coverage, not the exposure as a factor.
Viewer brightness is a viewing condition, not an exposure factor.
Cassette weight is not an exposure factor.

content.stem: For an X-ray exposure, the quantity of radiation delivered is set by the:
content.explanation: mA times time gives the quantity (mAs). kV sets the energy. Both, with distance, determine the exposure.
distractors: kV sets energy, not the total quantity by itself.
Film grain affects detail and speed, not the delivered quantity.
Distance affects intensity at the film but is not the quantity produced by the tube.

content.stem: By the inverse square law, doubling the source-to-film distance changes the beam intensity at the film to:
content.explanation: Intensity falls with the square of distance, so twice the distance gives one quarter the intensity, requiring about four times the exposure time to keep the same density.
distractors: Intensity falls with the square of distance, so it is one quarter, not half.
Greater distance lowers, not raises, intensity.
Intensity decreases with distance; it does not quadruple.

content.stem: If distance is doubled, the exposure time to keep the same density must be:
content.explanation: Because intensity drops to one quarter, time is increased about four times to maintain the same density at the greater distance.
distractors: Time must increase, not decrease, at greater distance.
Distance changes require a time change to hold density.
Time must increase about four times, not be reduced.

content.stem: An exposure (technique) chart relates kV or source, thickness, and distance to the:
options: Exposure time needed for proper density
The acceptance criteria for the part
content.explanation: Charts give a starting exposure for a material, thickness, energy, distance, and film to achieve the required density, refined by experience.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the code, not an exposure chart.
Record retention is unrelated to the exposure chart.
A survey-meter reading is a safety measurement, not a chart output.

content.stem: Increasing the exposure (more mAs or time) generally:
content.explanation: More radiation reaching the film increases development and density. Too little gives a thin (light) radiograph; too much gives an overly dark one.
distractors: More exposure darkens, not lightens, the film.
Exposure strongly affects density.
Exposure does not change the part thickness.

content.stem: A thicker or denser section requires:
options: More exposure to reach the same density
content.explanation: More material attenuates more radiation, so a longer exposure or higher energy is needed to reach the required density.
distractors: Thicker sections need more, not less, exposure.
An exposure is still required for thicker sections.
Film size does not substitute for the needed exposure.

content.stem: As a gamma source decays, to keep the same density the operator must:
content.explanation: Lower activity delivers less radiation per minute, so exposure time is increased, using the current source activity in the calculation.
distractors: Decaying activity needs more, not less, time.
Increasing distance would lower intensity further, worsening the density loss.
Decay must be compensated, not ignored.

content.stem: Compared with raising mA or time, a small increase in kV:
options: Has a large effect on penetration and density
content.explanation: kV changes both penetration and the quantity reaching the film, so small kV changes have a strong effect on density and contrast.
distractors: kV does affect penetration and density.
kV does not change the focal-spot size.
kV is not a tube-cooling control.

content.stem: Subject contrast comes mainly from differences in the part's thickness and density and the:
content.explanation: Subject contrast depends on how the material attenuates the beam, which depends on thickness, density, and the radiation energy. Lower energy raises subject contrast.
distractors: Exposure time affects density, not subject contrast.
Film size does not set subject contrast.
Viewer intensity is a viewing condition, not subject contrast.

content.stem: Film contrast depends mainly on the film type, the density, and the:
content.explanation: Film contrast is set by the film characteristics, the density achieved, and proper processing. Together with subject contrast it forms the radiographic contrast.
distractors: Source-to-film distance is geometry, not a film-contrast factor.
The collimator opening affects scatter and coverage, not film contrast.
A survey-meter reading is a safety measurement, not film contrast.

content.stem: Selecting a higher radiation energy generally:
options: Lowers subject contrast but increases penetration
content.explanation: Higher energy penetrates more but flattens density differences, lowering subject contrast. Lower energy raises contrast but penetrates less.
distractors: Higher energy lowers contrast while increasing penetration, not both up.
Energy does affect subject contrast.
An image medium is still required.

content.stem: Increasing the source-to-film distance generally:
options: Improves sharpness and reduces magnification, needing more exposure
Has no effect on the image
content.explanation: A longer distance reduces geometric unsharpness and magnification but lowers intensity, so exposure must increase per the inverse square law.
distractors: Greater distance improves, not reduces, sharpness.
Greater distance lengthens, not shortens, exposure.
Distance affects sharpness, magnification, and exposure.

content.stem: Image magnification increases when the:
options: Object is farther from the film (larger object-to-film distance)
content.explanation: A gap between the object and film magnifies and blurs the image, so the part is placed as close to the film as practical.
distractors: Placing the object on the film minimizes magnification.
With the source off there is no image.
Film speed does not control magnification.

content.stem: Film density is measured with a:
content.explanation: A densitometer reads the optical density of the processed film to confirm it falls within the required range.
distractors: A survey meter measures radiation, not film density.
A collimator shapes the beam, not measures density.
A crank handle drives the source; it does not measure density.

content.stem: Codes specify an acceptable film density range so the radiograph is:
options: Neither too light nor too dark to interpret
content.explanation: Density must fall within a specified range so detail is visible. A common minimum is about 1.8 for X-ray and about 2.0 for gamma (for example ASME Section V), with a typical maximum near 4.0. Confirm the exact range against the governing code.
distractors: Excessive darkness can hide detail and exceed the range.
Too light a radiograph lacks adequate density.
Density must be within the specified range, not any value.

content.stem: A gamma exposure calculation generally uses the source activity, the distance, and the:
content.explanation: Activity, distance (inverse square), and time set the exposure for a gamma source, adjusted as the source decays.
distractors: Film size affects coverage, not the exposure calculation.
Viewer brightness is a viewing condition, not part of the calculation.
Cassette type is not part of the gamma exposure calculation.

content.stem: A film characteristic (H and D) curve plots density against:
content.explanation: The characteristic curve shows how density rises with log exposure, describing the film's speed, contrast, and latitude. Level I uses it conceptually.
distractors: The curve plots density versus log exposure, not distance.
Focal-spot size affects sharpness, not the characteristic curve.
Collimator angle is not plotted on the characteristic curve.

content.stem: An underexposed radiograph is typically:
options: Too light, lacking density for interpretation
content.explanation: Too little exposure gives low density (too light), hiding detail. The exposure is increased to bring density into range.
distractors: Too dark indicates overexposure, not underexposure.
Underexposed film is not properly exposed.
An underexposed film still holds a faint image.

content.stem: An overexposed radiograph is typically:
options: Too dark, with density above the usable range
content.explanation: Excess exposure gives high density (too dark), and detail may be unreadable on a standard viewer. Exposure is reduced or a higher-density viewer used within limits.
distractors: Too light indicates underexposure, not overexposure.
Overexposure is not ideal.
An overexposed film is dark, not blank.

content.stem: When the correct exposure is uncertain, a technician may:
options: Bracket exposures to find the one giving proper density
content.explanation: Taking exposures above and below an estimate (bracketing) helps find the setting that yields acceptable density, refining the technique chart.
distractors: A single guess risks an unusable density.
Skipping the exposure produces no radiograph.
An image medium is required.

content.stem: For direct-exposure (lead-screen) film, intensity and time can be traded because the:
options: Product of intensity and time controls the exposure
content.explanation: With lead-screen film, the same density results from the same intensity-time product, so a lower intensity can be balanced by a longer time within limits.
distractors: Time strongly affects the exposure.
Intensity strongly affects the exposure.
The film is exposed by the radiation.

content.stem: Placing the part as close to the film as possible:
content.explanation: Minimizing the object-to-film distance keeps the image sharp and close to true size. An exposure is still required.
distractors: Closeness reduces, not increases, magnification.
Exposure is still needed.
Object position does not charge the source.

content.stem: For a thicker steel section, the operator generally selects:
options: A higher energy (higher kV or a higher-energy source)
content.explanation: Greater thickness needs more penetration, so a higher energy is chosen within the procedure, balancing contrast.
distractors: Thicker sections need higher, not lower, energy.
Radiation is required to penetrate the section.
Darkroom size does not affect penetration.

content.stem: To reduce scatter reaching the film during exposure, the technician may use:
options: Lead screens, collimation, masking, and backscatter lead
content.explanation: Collimation, lead screens, masking around the part, and a lead backing reduce scatter that would otherwise lower contrast.
distractors: Adding scatter degrades the image.
Film speed alone does not control scatter.
The safelight is a darkroom item, not a scatter control during exposure.

content.stem: A lead letter B placed behind the cassette that appears as a light image warns of:
content.explanation: If the B shows lighter on the darker film, backscatter is reaching the film from behind, and lead backing or shielding is added to control it.
distractors: A visible B image indicates a scatter problem, not a correct exposure.
It does not indicate film contact quality.
It does not indicate a dead source.

content.stem: Across a part of varying thickness, a single exposure may give:
options: Different densities in thick and thin areas
content.explanation: Thick areas pass less radiation (lighter) and thin areas pass more (darker), so multiple exposures or wide-latitude film may be needed for full coverage.
distractors: Varying thickness gives varying, not equal, density.
An image still forms across the thickness range.
Radiographs are grayscale, not colored.

content.stem: A longer exposure time at a gamma source means the source is exposed for longer, which:
options: Increases the radiation area duration and must be planned for safety
content.explanation: While the source is out, the surrounding area is a radiation hazard, so longer exposures mean longer controlled-area times, planned within safety procedures.
distractors: Longer exposure does have a safety implication.
Exposure time does not cool the source.
Exposure time affects density, not image sharpness, which is set by geometry.

content.stem: Exposure parameters used (energy, time, distance) should be:
options: Recorded so the radiograph can be reproduced and verified
content.explanation: Documenting the technique supports repeatability, troubleshooting density problems, and traceability.
distractors: Memory is not a reliable record of the technique.
Parameters are recorded, not discarded.
Parameters are set by the procedure, not random.

content.stem: Moving from 24 inches to 48 inches source-to-film, the exposure time should be multiplied by about:
content.explanation: Doubling the distance quarters the intensity, so time is multiplied by about four to hold the same density, by the inverse square law.
distractors: Doubling distance requires four times the time, not two.
Time increases, not halves, with greater distance.
Time increases by about four times, not decreases to one quarter.

content.stem: If a radiograph comes out too dark (density above range), the technician should:
options: Reduce the exposure (less time or mAs) and reshoot
content.explanation: Lowering the exposure brings density back into range. Shipping an out-of-range radiograph or changing the safelight does not fix the density.
distractors: More exposure makes it darker, worsening the problem.
An out-of-range radiograph should not be accepted as is.
The safelight does not affect exposure density.

content.stem: Choosing energy involves a trade-off because higher energy gives more penetration but:
content.explanation: The technician balances penetration against contrast, often using the lowest energy that adequately penetrates to keep contrast high.
distractors: Higher energy lowers, not raises, contrast.
An image still forms at higher energy.
Energy choice does not involve magnetism.

content.stem: In making exposures, the Level I technician:
options: Applies the technique and records it under direction
content.explanation: A Level I sets up and makes the exposure per the technique and records it; criteria, procedure approval, and evaluation are higher-level tasks.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Procedure approval is above the Level I.
Evaluating to code is a Level II responsibility.

content.stem: Which statement about exposure is correct?
options: Energy, intensity, time, and distance set the exposure; distance follows the inverse square law and controls density and sharpness
kV has no effect on density
content.explanation: Exposure depends on energy, intensity, time, and distance, with distance following the inverse square law, all set to achieve a density within the required range.
distractors: kV strongly affects density.
Distance affects intensity, density, and sharpness.
Film density is measured with a densitometer.

content.stem: Geometric unsharpness (Ug) is the blurring caused by the:
options: Finite size of the source and the object-to-film geometry
content.explanation: Because the source has a finite size, edges cast a penumbra. Ug grows with source size and object-to-film distance and shrinks with source-to-object distance.
distractors: Film grain affects detail but is separate from geometric unsharpness.
Developer temperature is a processing factor, not geometric unsharpness.
A survey meter measures radiation, not unsharpness.

content.stem: Geometric unsharpness is reduced by using a:
options: Smaller source, larger source-to-object distance, and smaller object-to-film distance
content.explanation: A small focal spot or source, more distance to the object, and the part close to the film all reduce penumbra and sharpen the image.
distractors: A larger source increases unsharpness.
A shorter source-to-object distance increases unsharpness.
A larger object-to-film gap increases unsharpness.

content.stem: Geometric unsharpness increases when the:
options: Film is placed against the part
content.explanation: Ug equals the source size times object-to-film distance divided by source-to-object distance, so a larger object-to-film distance raises it.
distractors: A larger source-to-object distance lowers Ug.
A smaller source lowers Ug.
Placing film against the part lowers Ug.

content.stem: The source-to-film distance is the sum of the:
content.explanation: The total source-to-film distance equals the source-to-object distance plus the object-to-film distance, which together set geometry and exposure.
distractors: Film dimensions are not the source-to-film distance.
kV and mA are exposure settings, not distances.
Half-life and time are not the geometric distances.

content.stem: An image quality indicator (IQI) is placed in the radiograph to:
options: Demonstrate the radiographic sensitivity (image quality) achieved
content.explanation: The IQI shows whether the technique resolves a required small detail, indicating the sensitivity of the radiograph. It does not measure dose or process film.
distractors: A survey meter measures dose, not the IQI.
The IQI does not collimate the beam.
The IQI is not operator shielding.

content.stem: A hole-type (plaque) IQI is a thin plaque containing:
content.explanation: The hole-type IQI has a known thickness and drilled holes sized relative to its thickness; seeing a required hole demonstrates sensitivity.
distractors: A single wire describes a wire-type IQI, not a plaque.
An IQI does not contain developer.
An IQI contains no radiation source.

content.stem: A wire-type IQI consists of:
options: A set of wires of graded diameters
content.explanation: Wire IQIs hold several wires of increasing diameter; the thinnest wire visible indicates the sensitivity achieved.
distractors: A plaque with holes is the hole-type IQI, not a wire IQI.
A lead letter B is a backscatter indicator, not a wire IQI.
A step wedge is a density reference, not a wire IQI.

content.stem: The IQI material should be:
options: The same or radiographically similar to the part material
content.explanation: The IQI is selected from the same material group (or a radiographically similar one) so its response represents the part. Lead and random materials would not.
distractors: Lead is not used as the IQI body; it would not represent the part.
A random metal may not be radiographically similar to the part.
Plastic does not represent a metal part radiographically.

content.stem: The IQI is preferably placed on the:
content.explanation: Source-side placement represents the worst-case image quality through the full thickness. Film-side placement is allowed when access requires it, marked with an F.
distractors: Film-side placement is a permitted alternative, not the preference.
The IQI must be in the beam to appear on the image.
The IQI is placed on the part, not on the tube.

content.stem: When an IQI must be placed on the film side, the radiograph is marked with a:
options: Lead letter F next to the IQI
content.explanation: An F marker shows the IQI was on the film side, since that location reads slightly more sensitive than source side and must be known to the interpreter.
distractors: The letter B indicates backscatter, not film-side IQI.
A survey reading is a safety measurement, not an IQI marker.
A density number is a measurement, not the film-side marker.

content.stem: Radiographic sensitivity expressed as a percentage describes the:
options: Smallest thickness change that can be detected, as a percent of thickness
content.explanation: Better sensitivity means a smaller detectable thickness change, so a lower percentage is better. It is demonstrated by the IQI.
distractors: Sensitivity here is not source activity.
Film speed is a separate property.
Darkroom brightness is unrelated to sensitivity.

content.stem: A 2 percent radiographic sensitivity is:
options: Better than 4 percent (detects a smaller change)
content.explanation: A lower percentage means a smaller detectable thickness change, so 2 percent sensitivity is better than 4 percent.
distractors: A lower percent is better, so 2 percent is not worse than 4 percent.
2 percent and 4 percent are not the same sensitivity.
Sensitivity percentage directly relates to detectability.

content.stem: The essential hole or essential wire is the:
options: Specific IQI feature that must be visible to meet the required quality level
content.explanation: The procedure specifies an IQI level (for example 2-2T), and the named essential hole or wire must be visible on the radiograph to pass the quality check.
distractors: The required feature is specified, not simply the largest hole.
It is an image-quality requirement, not a source-side marker.
It is not the film identification number.

content.stem: A 2-2T quality level means an IQI of about 2 percent of part thickness with the:
content.explanation: The first number is the IQI thickness as a percent of part thickness; 2T names the hole (twice the IQI thickness) that must be visible. Exact requirements come from the code.
distractors: The 2-2T level requires the 2T hole, not only the larger 4T hole.
A hole must be visible to demonstrate quality.
The IQI feature must be present and visible, not removed.

content.stem: When a hole-type IQI sits on a thinner area or the film side, a shim may be used to:
options: Represent the correct material thickness under the IQI
content.explanation: A shim of similar material makes the IQI represent the intended thickness so the demonstrated sensitivity is valid for the part.
distractors: A shim is not used to add scatter.
A shim supports the IQI; it does not replace it.
Location marking is a separate identification step, not the shim's role.

content.stem: Lead location markers are placed on the part and imaged so that:
options: Indications can be located back on the actual part
content.explanation: Location markers tie positions on the radiograph to positions on the part, so an indication can be found and addressed on the hardware.
distractors: Markers serve location, not decoration.
Markers do not shield the source.
Markers do not set the kV.

content.stem: Lead identification markers on the radiograph provide:
options: Traceability to the part, weld, and date
content.explanation: Identification markers (numbers and letters) make each radiograph traceable to the specific item, location, and time, a requirement for records.
distractors: Markers are lead identification, not operator shielding.
Markers do not collimate the beam.
Markers do not cool the source.

content.stem: A single-wall single-image (SWSI) technique passes the beam through:
options: One wall, with the image of that wall on the film
content.explanation: In SWSI the beam penetrates a single wall and images it, used where the inside is accessible for film or the source.
distractors: Imaging both walls on one film describes a double-wall technique.
The beam must pass through the wall to image it.
The technique images the part wall, not the source.

content.stem: A double-wall single-image (DWSI) technique is used when:
options: Only the wall nearest the film is interpreted, beam through both walls
The source is inside a casting
content.explanation: DWSI shoots through both walls of a pipe but interprets the wall near the film, common where the bore is not accessible.
distractors: DWSI applies to hollow sections like pipe, not solid parts.
Film is used to capture the image.
DWSI does not require the source inside a casting.

content.stem: A double-wall double-image (DWDI) technique on small-diameter pipe images:
options: Both walls on one film, often as an ellipse
content.explanation: On small pipe, DWDI superimposes or offsets both walls (often an elliptical shot) so the weld is interpreted on a single film. The procedure sets diameter limits.
distractors: DWDI images both walls, not only one.
The technique images the weld, not nothing.
It images the pipe weld, not the darkroom.

content.stem: When multiple films cover a long weld, the films should:
options: Overlap so no length is left unexamined
content.explanation: Overlapping film coverage, with location markers, ensures the entire weld length is radiographed with no gaps.
distractors: Gaps would leave weld length unexamined.
One spot is not full coverage.
Weld ends must be covered, not avoided.

content.stem: The IQI on each radiograph confirms that the:
options: Required image quality was achieved for that exposure
content.explanation: Seeing the required IQI feature confirms the technique met the specified quality level for that radiograph.
distractors: The IQI does not indicate source decay.
The IQI does not verify the darkroom.
Film color is not what the IQI confirms.

content.stem: Two parts of radiographic image quality are contrast and:
content.explanation: Image quality combines contrast (density differences) and definition (sharpness, governed by geometry and film). The IQI helps demonstrate both are adequate.
distractors: Source activity affects exposure, not the image-quality pair with contrast.
Exposure time affects density, not the definition element of image quality.
Film size affects coverage, not image-quality definition.

content.stem: For the sharpest image, the ideal source approaches a:
options: Point source (very small focal spot or source size)
content.explanation: The closer the source is to a point, the smaller the penumbra and the sharper the image, which is why small focal spots are valued.
distractors: A large area source increases blur.
Safelights are darkroom lighting, not the radiation source.
A sound emitter is not a radiographic source.

content.stem: Increasing the source-to-object distance to improve sharpness also:
content.explanation: More distance lowers intensity, so exposure time rises, a trade-off against the sharper geometry it provides.
distractors: Greater distance lengthens, not shortens, exposure.
Distance does not magnetize the part.
Distance does not develop the film.

content.stem: Codes specify how many IQIs are needed based on the:
options: Length and geometry of the area radiographed
content.explanation: The number and placement of IQIs depend on the radiograph length and geometry so quality is demonstrated across the coverage. Follow the governing code.
distractors: Exposure time does not set the number of IQIs.
Film density is a result to verify, not the basis for IQI count.
Source-to-film distance does not set the IQI count.

content.stem: Source-side IQI placement is preferred because it represents the:
options: More demanding (worst-case) image quality through the thickness
content.explanation: Image quality is harder to achieve on the source side, so demonstrating it there assures the rest of the thickness meets the level.
distractors: Source side is worst-case, not best-case.
IQI placement represents image quality, not just density.
IQI placement represents image quality through the thickness, not source energy.

content.stem: Lead masking or blocking around the part during exposure helps:
options: Reduce scatter and undercut at edges
content.explanation: Masking absorbs radiation that would otherwise scatter around thin edges and degrade the image, improving edge definition.
distractors: Masking does not increase magnification.
Masking does not develop film.
Masking does not charge the source.

content.stem: The radiographic technique (SWSI, DWSI, DWDI) is chosen based on the:
content.explanation: Access to the bore, diameter, and geometry determine whether single-wall or double-wall techniques are used, per the procedure.
distractors: Density target is achieved by exposure, not the basis for technique choice.
Exposure time is set after the technique, not the basis for it.
Viewer brightness is a viewing condition, not the basis for technique.

content.stem: If the required IQI hole or wire is not visible, the radiograph:
options: Does not meet the quality level and is generally reshot
content.explanation: Failing to show the essential IQI feature means the technique did not achieve the required sensitivity, so the cause is corrected and the radiograph retaken.
distractors: A failed IQI means the radiograph is not acceptable.
An invalid radiograph does not prove the part sound.
Action is required when the IQI level is not met.

content.stem: IQI type, location, and any shim used should be:
options: Recorded as part of the radiographic technique
content.explanation: Documenting the IQI and placement lets the interpreter confirm the demonstrated quality and supports traceability.
distractors: IQI details are documented, not left out.
IQI selection follows the code, not randomness.
The interpreter needs the IQI details, not hidden ones.

content.stem: In setting up geometry and IQIs, the Level I technician:
options: Places IQIs and markers and sets geometry per the procedure under direction
content.explanation: A Level I follows the procedure to set geometry, place IQIs and markers, and shoot; defining criteria, approving techniques, and interpreting are higher-level tasks.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving the technique sheet is above the Level I.
Interpreting to code is a Level II responsibility.

content.stem: Sharp radiographs are favored by a small source, a long source-to-object distance, and the part:
content.explanation: Small source, long source-to-object distance, and minimal object-to-film distance together minimize geometric unsharpness.
distractors: Placing the part far from the film increases blur and magnification.
The part must be in the beam to be imaged.
Wrapping the part in lead would block the image.

content.stem: Which statement about geometry, technique, and IQIs is correct?
options: Geometry controls sharpness, the technique suits the part, and the IQI demonstrates the achieved sensitivity
A larger source gives sharper images
A higher sensitivity percentage is better
content.explanation: Source size and distances govern sharpness, the shooting technique fits the geometry, and the IQI confirms the required image quality, with lower sensitivity percentages being better.
distractors: The IQI demonstrates image quality, not radiation dose.
A larger source gives blurrier, not sharper, images.
A lower sensitivity percentage is better, not higher.

content.stem: The basic manual film processing sequence is:
options: Develop, stop or rinse, fix, wash, dry
content.explanation: The exposed film is developed, the development is stopped, the film is fixed, washed, and dried, in that order.
distractors: Fixing comes after developing, and exposure happens before processing.
Exposure precedes processing; washing is near the end.
Developing precedes fixing, and drying is last.

content.stem: The developer:
options: Converts exposed silver halide to black metallic silver
content.explanation: Development reduces the exposed grains to metallic silver, forming the visible dark image. Removing unexposed halide is the fixer's job.
distractors: Removing unexposed halide is the fixer's role, not the developer's.
Stopping action is the stop bath's role.
Drying is a later step, not the developer's role.

content.stem: The fixer:
options: Removes undeveloped silver halide and makes the image permanent
content.explanation: Fixing clears the unexposed, undeveloped halide so the film is no longer light-sensitive and the image is stable.
distractors: Darkening exposed areas is the developer's action.
The fixer stops, not speeds, development.
The fixer clears halide; it does not add image density.

content.stem: The stop bath or rinse between developer and fixer:
options: Halts development and protects the fixer
content.explanation: The stop or rinse step ends development at the right time and reduces carryover of developer into the fixer.
distractors: Development begins in the developer, not the stop bath.
Drying is the final step, not the stop bath.
The film is exposed before processing, not at the stop bath.

content.stem: The final wash removes:
options: Residual chemicals that would stain or fade the image
content.explanation: Washing clears leftover fixer and chemicals; inadequate washing causes staining and long-term fading of the radiograph.
distractors: Washing preserves, not removes, the silver image.
Washing does not remove the film base.
Washing does not strip the emulsion.

content.stem: Manual development is controlled by:
content.explanation: Density and contrast depend on both development time and temperature; warmer developer acts faster, so both are controlled to a standard.
distractors: Temperature matters too; time alone is not enough.
Time matters too; temperature alone is not enough.
Source exposure sets the latent image; development is controlled by developer time and temperature.

content.stem: An automatic film processor:
options: Transports film through the chemicals at controlled time and temperature
Develops film in daylight without chemicals
content.explanation: Automatic processors move film through developer, fixer, wash, and dryer at set times and temperatures for consistent results.
distractors: Processors still use chemicals and a light-tight feed.
A processor does not replace the radiation source.
A processor does not measure dose.

content.stem: A darkroom safelight must have the correct filter, wattage, and distance so that it:
options: Provides light without fogging the film
Fully lights the room in white
